say.en: No species lives alone. Even a plant needs soil microbes and pollinators. Every pair of species interacts, and each interaction can help, harm or leave a species unaffected. In this lesson: Classify population interactions by their effect (plus, minus, 0).
Explain the roles of predators and prey defences.
Explain competition, competitive exclusion and resource partitioning.

body.en: Interspecific *interactions* arise between populations of two different species and can be beneficial (+), detrimental (−) or neutral (0) to each. Mutualism: + / +. Competition: − / −. Predation and parasitism: + / −. Commensalism: + / 0. Amensalism: − / 0. Predation transfers energy fixed by plants to higher trophic levels. Predators keep prey populations under control: when the prickly pear cactus was introduced into Australia in the early 1920s it spread rapidly, and was brought under control only after a cactus-feeding predator (a moth) from its natural habitat was introduced; biological control of pests is based on this. Predators also maintain species diversity by reducing competition among prey: in American Pacific coast rocky intertidal communities, the starfish Pisaster is an important predator; when all starfish were removed from an enclosed area, more than 10 species of invertebrates became extinct within a year because of interspecific competition. Prey defend themselves: some insects and frogs are cryptically coloured (camouflaged); the Monarch butterfly is highly distasteful because of a chemical it acquires by feeding on a poisonous weed as a caterpillar. Nearly 25 per cent of all insects are phytophagous; plants defend themselves with thorns (Acacia, cactus) and chemicals: Calotropis makes highly poisonous cardiac glycosides, and nicotine, caffeine, quinine, strychnine and opium are produced as defences against grazers and browsers.

points.en: Prickly pear in Australia controlled by a cactus-feeding moth
Removing Pisaster → >10 invertebrate species extinct in a year
Defences: camouflage, Monarch's distaste, thorns, cardiac glycosides of Calotropis

caption.en: Prey grow towards their carrying capacity; predators eat them and multiply. The prey peak comes first and the predator peak follows, and the swings settle down. Without predators, prey rise to the limit set by food: predators keep prey populations in check, as the cactus moth did for the prickly pear in Australia. A simple model.

body.en: Darwin was convinced that interspecific *competition* is a potent force in organic evolution. Competition occurs when closely related species compete for the same limited resources, but totally unrelated species can also compete: flamingoes and resident fishes compete for their common food, the zooplankton, in some shallow South American lakes. Resources need not be limiting: in interference competition, the feeding efficiency of one species may be reduced by the inhibitory presence of the other. The Abingdon tortoise in the Galapagos Islands became extinct within a decade after goats were introduced, apparently because of the greater browsing efficiency of the goats. Competitive release: a species whose distribution is restricted by a competitively superior species expands its range when the competitor is removed. Connell's field experiments on the rocky sea coasts of Scotland showed that the larger, competitively superior barnacle Balanus dominates the intertidal area and excludes the smaller barnacle Chthamalus from that zone. Gause's competitive exclusion principle states that two closely related species competing for the same resources cannot co-exist indefinitely, and the competitively inferior one will be eliminated eventually. Species facing competition may evolve mechanisms for co-existence, such as resource partitioning: MacArthur showed that five closely related species of warblers living on the same tree avoided competition and co-existed because of behavioural differences in their foraging activities.

points.en: Flamingoes vs fishes for zooplankton (unrelated species)
Abingdon tortoise extinct after goats introduced

narration.en: In competition both species lose. Gause's principle says two closely related species using the same resources cannot co-exist forever; Connell's barnacles show Balanus excluding Chthamalus. MacArthur's warblers co-exist on one tree by foraging differently: resource partitioning.

myth.en: Competition happens only between closely related species, and only when food runs short.

truth.en: Unrelated species compete too (flamingoes and fishes), and competition can occur with plenty of resources, through interference. Gause's principle is about closely related species, which is why students over-generalise it. NCERT defines competition by its effect, lowered fitness, not by relatedness or scarcity.

say.en: Mutualism +/+, competition −/−, predation and parasitism +/−, commensalism +/0, amensalism −/0.

Gause's competitive exclusion principle; resource partitioning in MacArthur's warblers; competitive release in Connell's barnacles.

Mutualism: lichens, mycorrhizae, fig–wasp, Ophrys and bee (sexual deceit).

problem.en: Classify each interaction with +, − or 0: (a) a tiger eats a deer; (b) goats and the Abingdon tortoise feed on the same plants; (c) flamingoes and fishes in a lake eat the same zooplankton.

steps.en: (a) The tiger gains (+), the deer is harmed (−): predation, + / −.
(b) Both share limited food and both are harmed: competition, − / −.
(c) Unrelated species, same food: still competition, − / −.

narration.en: Let us work through this together. Classify each interaction with +, − or 0: (a) a tiger eats a deer; (b) goats and the Abingdon tortoise feed on the same plants; (c) flamingoes and fishes in a lake eat the same zooplankton.

say.en: Let us work through this together. Classify each interaction with plus, - or 0: a a tiger eats a deer; b goats and the Abingdon tortoise feed on the same plants; c flamingoes and fishes in a lake eat the same zooplankton.
a The tiger gains plus, the deer is harmed (-): predation, plus / minus.
b Both share limited food and both are harmed: competition, - / minus.
c Unrelated species, same food: still competition, - / minus.
So the answer is a predation (plus /-); b competition (-/-); c competition (-/-).

narration.kn: ಪುನರಾವರ್ತನೆ. ಪರಸ್ಪರ ಕ್ರಿಯೆಗಳು: ಸಹೋಪಕಾರ ++, ಸ್ಪರ್ಧೆ −−, ಭಕ್ಷಣೆ/ಪರಾವಲಂಬನೆ +−, ಸಹಭೋಜನ +0, ಅಮೆನ್ಸಲಿಸಂ −0. ಭಕ್ಷಕಗಳು ಬೇಟೆಯನ್ನು ನಿಯಂತ್ರಿಸುತ್ತವೆ (ಆಸ್ಟ್ರೇಲಿಯಾದ ಪಾಪಾಸುಕಳ್ಳಿ) ಮತ್ತು ವೈವಿಧ್ಯ ಕಾಪಾಡುತ್ತವೆ (ಪಿಸಾಸ್ಟರ್). ಬೇಟೆಯ ರಕ್ಷಣೆ: ಮರೆಮಾಚುವಿಕೆ, ಅರುಚಿ, ಮುಳ್ಳುಗಳು ಮತ್ತು ವಿಷ ರಾಸಾಯನಿಕಗಳು. ಗಾಸ್ ತತ್ವ; ಕಾನೆಲ್‌ರ ಬಾರ್ನಕಲ್‌ಗಳು; ಮ್ಯಾಕ್‌ಆರ್ಥರ್‌ರ ವಾರ್ಬ್ಲರ್‌ಗಳು ಸಂಪನ್ಮೂಲ ಹಂಚಿಕೆ ತೋರಿಸುತ್ತವೆ.

say.en: Let us recall the key ideas. Interactions: mutualism plus plus, competition --, predation/parasitism plus minus, commensalism plus 0, amensalism minus 0.
